export const meta = {
  name: 'lane-repair-design',
  description: 'Judge panel: three independent designs for repairing one lane of a blocked workflow run, scored and synthesized into a design doc',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Design', detail: 'three designers, different angles' },
    { title: 'Judge', detail: 'score and synthesize the recommended design' },
  ],
}

const REPO = '/home/agentops/dev/md-manager'
const CONTEXT = `Repository: ${REPO} (Python package workflow/, the LangGraph-based automatic controller; read workflow/README.md and workflow/RUNBOOK.md first, then workflow/pipeline.py, workflow/automatic.py, workflow/sessions.py, workflow/interactive.py, workflow/checks.py, workflow/verification.py, workflow/integration*.py or wherever the candidate is built). Read-only: do not edit anything in the repository or any run directory; do not run git commands that change state; no tests needed.

Problem (from /home/agentops/dev/md-manager-reviews/workflow-guardrails-001-issues.md, P1 'the verifier's browser rules are hidden from the lanes until the candidate', third bullet): in run workflow-guardrails-001 (run dir ~/.local/state/md-manager-workflows/workflow-guardrails/workflow-guardrails-001; read its plan.json, events.jsonl, verification/*/*/*/packet.json, attempts.json, checkpoint files as examples) both lanes finished and passed worker-phase verification, the combined candidate was integrated, and the candidate check of the ui lane failed twice identically on a one-line test defect ('Expected one screenshot attachment for inert-markdown'). The worker sessions had been stopped and their snapshots frozen; the identical-failure guard ended the run blocked. There is no supported way to send one lane back for a fix: \`retry\` reruns checks at the same revision and never launches a worker; \`reconcile\` never launches. The operator had to finish by hand outside the workflow. The same dead end exists when a lane blocks in the worker phase.

Prior art: an unmerged commit 312a96d on branch fix/worker-relaunch ('Add workflow relaunch for a stopped worker lane': \`git -C ${REPO} show 312a96d\`) relaunches a halted lane BEFORE handoff (archives the attempt under relaunched/<lane>/<attempt>/, one new session with the same task in the same worktree, fresh deadline; refuses lanes that already handed off, whose stop is unconfirmed or whose session is alive). The codebase deliberately says 'no automatic relaunch' in many places: repairs must be operator-initiated and auditable.

Invariants that any design must keep (check the code for more): a worker/reviewer session is launched at most once per recorded launch intent and never implicitly; frozen snapshots are immutable evidence (a repair produces a NEW snapshot, never rewrites one); every lane snapshot touches only its owned paths; the trusted verifier re-runs every policy check on each new snapshot and on each new candidate; reviewers only ever see a candidate that passed; the source checkout is pinned and stays clean until integration; everything is resumable after a crash at any point; the viewer/export can show what happened (export_state.py).

Produce a concrete design: the operator command(s) and flags, which states they accept and refuse, exactly which run files/graph state change (LangGraph checkpoint handling: rewind/update_state vs new thread vs new sub-run), how the new snapshot is produced (a new worker session in the lane worktree seeded with the blocking reasons and the original task, and/or an operator-supplied commit), how verification attempts, candidate numbering, attempts.json and the identical-failure guard are reset or archived, how the export/timeline shows it, crash points and recovery, the test list, and an honest size estimate (files, lines, test count). Name the simplest version that would have saved workflow-guardrails-001.`

const ANGLES = [
  { key: 'operator-amend', angle: 'Design angle: SIMPLEST FIRST. Prefer an operator-supplied fix: e.g. `workflow amend <run> <lane> <commit>` where the operator (or a Claude session they run by hand) commits a fix on top of the lane snapshot; the controller validates ancestry and owned paths, records it as the lane\'s next snapshot and re-enters worker-phase verification and candidate integration. Consider whether a worker relaunch is needed at all.' },
  { key: 'worker-relaunch', angle: 'Design angle: AUTOMATE THE REPAIR WITH A WORKER. Extend 312a96d into `workflow relaunch <run> <lane>` that also works after handoff/freeze and after a candidate block: a new worker session in the lane worktree whose task is the original task plus the verifier\'s blocking reasons (and the failing evidence paths), then the normal completion, freeze, worker verification, candidate integration and review flow.' },
  { key: 'risk-first', angle: 'Design angle: RISK FIRST. Start from the invariants and crash points and from how LangGraph checkpoints are used in this code; design the state transitions so a repair can never mix old and new evidence, never launch twice, and is resumable at every step; then decide which command surface (amend, relaunch, or both sharing one state transition) that safely supports, and what to refuse.' },
]

const DESIGN = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    title: { type: 'string' },
    summary: { type: 'string' },
    commands: { type: 'string' },
    state_transitions: { type: 'string' },
    snapshot_and_verification: { type: 'string' },
    refusals: { type: 'string' },
    crash_recovery: { type: 'string' },
    export_and_timeline: { type: 'string' },
    tests: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
    size_estimate: { type: 'string' },
    minimal_version: { type: 'string' },
    risks: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
  required: ['title', 'summary', 'commands', 'state_transitions', 'snapshot_and_verification', 'refusals', 'crash_recovery', 'tests', 'size_estimate', 'minimal_version', 'risks'],
}

phase('Design')
const designs = (await parallel(ANGLES.map(a => () => agent(`${CONTEXT}\n\n${a.angle}`, { label: `design:${a.key}`, phase: 'Design', schema: DESIGN })
  .then(d => d && ({ key: a.key, ...d }))))).filter(Boolean)

phase('Judge')
const doc = await agent(`${CONTEXT}\n\nThree independent designers proposed these designs (JSON):\n${JSON.stringify(designs, null, 2)}\n\nYou are the judge. Verify the load-bearing claims of each against the code (read the functions they cite; reject designs built on wrong assumptions about how the pipeline, LangGraph checkpoints, snapshots or verification work). Score each on: safety against the invariants, crash recovery, operator simplicity, implementation size/risk, and whether it would have saved workflow-guardrails-001. Then write ONE recommended design, taking the best of each, with a clear minimal first version and what is deferred. Write it as Markdown to /home/agentops/dev/md-manager-reviews/lane-repair-design.md (this is the only file you may write) with sections: Recommendation (3-5 sentences), Scores (table), Command surface, State transitions, Snapshot and verification, Refusals, Crash recovery, Export and timeline, Tests, Size, Deferred, Rejected alternatives. Return the file path and a 10-line summary including the size estimate.`, { label: 'judge', phase: 'Judge' })
return { designs: designs.map(d => ({ key: d.key, title: d.title, summary: d.summary, size: d.size_estimate })), doc }

designs.title: workflow amend: an operator-supplied lane fix after freeze, re-verified through a LangGraph fork at the freeze boundary
designs.summary:
Add one operator command: `python -m workflow amend "$RUN" --commit <lane>=<sha> [...] --reason "<text>"`. It accepts a run that has been frozen and then blocked at a failed `verify_<lane>` step or `candidate` step, as long as no review bundle exists yet.

**How the operator supplies the fix.** The operator, or a Claude session they start by hand, commits the fix in a detached worktree. The commit sits on top of one of two things:
- the lane's frozen snapshot, or
- the current combined candidate. This is exactly what the operator did in workflow-guardrails-001: 7c5e37e's parent is candidate 1ab6b95.

**What the controller does, in order:**
1. Validates ancestry, lane ownership (the same rules as freeze), and that the pinned source checkout has not moved.
2. Builds a new snapshot commit whose parent is base, holding the lane's full tree. Parent = base matters because the candidate node cherry-picks one commit per lane.
3. Writes the change to an append-only journal, `amendments.json`.
4. Raises the attempt counters. The limit of 3 now applies per revision.
5. Forks the same LangGraph thread from the freeze-boundary checkpoint with `update_state(as_node="handoff")`.

**How the run continues.** `automatic "$RUN" --live` (or `retry "$RUN"` for a manual run) re-verifies every lane:
- The amended lane gets a fresh worker-phase attempt.
- The unchanged lanes reuse their packets after `recheck_packet`.
- The candidate is rebuilt as `candidate-a<n>` and every lane's candidate checks rerun.
- Reviewers see nothing until that candidate passes.

**What stays untouched.** `amend` never launches a session, never rewrites `snapshots.json`, `plan.json`, packets or refs, and never touches the source checkout.

**A finding that shaped the design.** I checked this against a scratch copy of 001's `pipeline.sqlite`; the run directory was not modified. Calling `update_state(as_node="handoff")` on the latest checkpoint is wrong: `next` becomes `(verify_controller, verify_ui, candidate)`. The failed `candidate` task's join trigger was never consumed, so it would run in the same step as re-verification, reading the old packets with the new, unverified snapshot. Forking from the newest checkpoint whose `next` is exactly the verify fan-out gives:
- `next == (verify_controller, verify_ui)`, `packets == {}` and no errors;
- the candidate then runs after both verifies, with the fresh packets;
- a second amendment correctly forks from the first amendment's head;
- the failed branch stays in history.

The probe scripts are `ckpt_probe.py`, `ckpt_hist.py` and `ckpt_fork2.py` in `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-agentops-dev-md-manager/7579e0f3-92af-47b0-b407-1cfb21a9be7a/scratchpad/`.

**Is a worker relaunch needed?** Not for this problem.
- The 001 fix was 2 insertions and 1 deletion.
- The prior art, 312a96d, is pre-handoff only. It also could not work live: `InteractiveSessions.run` refuses any dirty worktree ("Worktree changed since preparation"), and a halted worker's worktree is dirty. Its test used FakeSessions.
- A post-freeze relaunch would need a new launch authority: new launch names, a new worktree at the snapshot, archived completion files, a wait outside the handoff node, a stop, and a single-lane capture.

Build `amend` first. A repair worker can later produce a commit for the same apply path.

**Estimated size:** about 290 lines of code (a new `workflow/amend.py` plus small edits to `pipeline.py`, `automatic.py` and `__main__.py`), about 460 lines of tests (13 tests), and about 30 lines of RUNBOOK. No export-version bump is needed for the first version.

designs.title: Lane repair: `workflow relaunch <run> <lane>` starts one repair worker, freezes a new lane snapshot, forks the checkpoint back to verification and re-verifies everything
designs.summary:
Only the operator starts a repair. `python -m workflow relaunch RUN <lane>` records a repair intent (repair k) and launches exactly one new native worker session, node `repair-<k>`. Its task is the lane's original task, plus the verifier's blocking reasons verbatim, the failing packet, log and report paths, and an optional operator note. When the session writes a valid completion, the controller stops it and captures a NEW lane snapshot (parent = base, owned paths only). It then forks the LangGraph thread from the checkpoint just after the handoff, with the new snapshot map. From there the normal path reruns: worker verification of the new snapshot, a new candidate generation checked for every lane, review, and integration. Nothing that already exists is moved or rewritten.

What the code and the run workflow-guardrails-001 showed:
1. The ui lane cannot build in isolation. verification/worker/ui/1/check-0.log has 19 TS errors: contract fields that only the controller lane adds. The ui worker's completion says it had to stub the contract in a scratch copy to run Playwright. A repair worker inside worktree-ui could not reproduce the candidate failure. For a candidate block, the repair worktree must be a detached checkout of the failing combined candidate (1ab6b95).
2. I tested the rewind on the pinned langgraph 1.2.11, in the scratchpad, with the same history shape as this run's pipeline.sqlite (step 2 = verify fan-out with an errored verify, step 3 = errored candidate).
   - Calling update_state(head, {snapshots}, as_node='handoff') from the failed head is WRONG. The errored `candidate` task stays pending, so the candidate runs in the same superstep as the new verifies, using the stale ui packet, and then runs again.
   - Forking from the latest checkpoint whose `next` is exactly the verify fan-out is correct. It produces next = the verifies only, runs each verify once with the new snapshot, then runs the candidate once. The failed branch stays in history.
   - Forking from the interrupt checkpoint re-runs the handoff interrupt, so that is also wrong.
3. candidate() reuses candidate.json whenever it exists, and verify_revision refuses an attempt directory that belongs to another revision. A repair therefore needs generation paths (candidate-<g>.json, candidate-<g>/), attempt numbers that keep counting up, and per-generation floors for the attempt limit and the identical-failure guard.
4. plan.json cannot change: plan_digest is bound into every receipt, and locate() refuses on a mismatch. All repair state therefore lives in repairs.json and in repair-<k>.* files, mirroring how reviewers use review-<id>.* files.
5. Packets store absolute paths (artifact_root, artifact_paths, verification_cwd), and worktrees are registered with git. Archiving by moving would break recheck_packet and git's worktree metadata, so every change is additive.
6. Commit 312a96d has defects that stop it working live:
   - InteractiveSessions.run refuses a dirty worktree ('Worktree changed since preparation'), so a relaunch fails for any lane that has edits. FakeSessions skips that check, which hides it.
   - It refuses any lane with a completion file, including `status: blocked`, the most common block.
   - After a relaunch, wait_handoffs' stop.json recovery branch fails on a sibling that drive() had stopped (it has no handoff.json). drive() then calls stop_workers(), which stops the session that was just relaunched.
   The design keeps its refusals (stop confirmed, not handed off, not alive) but replaces archive-and-reuse with a repair node.

Scope by state:
- C, candidate block: the minimal version, and the one that would have saved 001.
- B, worker-phase verification block: nearly free once C exists.
- A, a lane blocked or stopped before handoff: supersedes 312a96d; needs changes to wait_handoffs and freeze.
- Out of scope for v1: repair after a review block; manual-mode runs.
- `--from-commit` is an operator-commit variant with no model usage. It would have accepted the operator's actual fix 7c5e37e unchanged, because its parent is exactly the candidate commit 1ab6b95.

designs.title: Lane repair for frozen runs: one `repair` state machine with amend and relaunch modes, a fresh LangGraph thread per repair generation, and repair-scoped evidence
designs.summary:
Nothing was edited. I read the workflow code, the run directory of workflow-guardrails-001 and prior-art commit 312a96d, and ran one LangGraph probe in the scratchpad.

**Recommendation.** Add one operator command, `repair`, backed by one file-journaled state machine that runs outside the graph. It has two ways to produce the new lane snapshot:
- **amend:** the operator edits a fresh repair worktree.
- **relaunch:** one new native worker session edits that worktree.

Both modes end in the same step: capture a NEW lane snapshot, then seed a NEW LangGraph thread (`<run_id>/repair-<n>`) as if `handoff` had just produced the new snapshots. The trusted verifier then re-runs everything through the unchanged graph: worker checks for the repaired lane, and every lane's checks on the new candidate. Review and approval follow as usual.

**Why a new thread (shown by the probe, not just argued).** Calling `update_state(as_node="handoff")` on the failed thread schedules `candidate` in the same superstep as the `verify_*` nodes. The verify→candidate join barrier is never consumed when `candidate` errors. In the probe, `candidate` ran with the new snapshots and the OLD packets (`p-b-B0`), then ran a second time. In this code base that would pair new snapshots with stale worker packets, or reuse the old `candidate.json`. The same call on an EMPTY thread gives `next = (verify_a, verify_b)` and a clean run, and leaves the old thread untouched as history. Rewind or fork within the same thread is rejected for the same reason: a fork from the failed checkpoint brings the hazard back, and nothing marks which branch is live.

**Why a new directory and not archive-and-reuse (as in 312a96d).**
- `plan.json` is immutable: every receipt stores `plan_digest` and `InteractiveSessions.locate` refuses if it changes. So no repair state can live in the plan.
- Frozen evidence stays where every current reader expects it. Everything the repair produces goes under `repairs/<n>/`.
- The repair session gets a unique launch token, launch name (`workflow-<run>-<lane>-repair-<n>`) and working directory. An old file can therefore never validate as a new one.

**Why a fresh worktree at the failing revision and not the lane worktree.**
- `InteractiveSessions.run` refuses a dirty lane worktree ("Worktree changed since preparation"), and `worktree-ui` in the 001 run is dirty.
- A lane worktree cannot build the combined application. In 001, worker/ui/1 recorded "frontend-build: exit 2" and "no Playwright report written", so a repair session there could not reproduce the candidate failure.
- For a candidate-phase failure, the repair worktree starts at the failing candidate commit, which is buildable. Because lane ownership is disjoint, the owned-path edits map exactly onto the lane snapshot.
- The operator's actual fix 7c5e37e has parent 1ab6b95, the failing candidate commit, so it is exactly this shape.

**Prior art 312a96d should not be merged as is.**
- Its `run()` refuses the dirty lane worktree.
- After one lane blocks, `drive()` stops every worker, so the other lanes have `stop.json`. `wait_handoffs` then takes its recovery branch, reads a missing completion or handoff, raises, and `drive()` calls `stop_workers` again, which kills the relaunched session.
- It reuses the same launch name and completion token.
- If it crashes after moving `stop.json` but before launching, it refuses forever with "No confirmed stop".
- Its questions and deadline files carry over from the old session.
- Its test used FakeSessions, so none of this was exercised.

**Minimal version:** amend only, for failed worker or candidate verification with no review bundle yet. It is about 550 lines of production code and 18 tests, and it would have saved workflow-guardrails-001 at 20:27.
designs.size:

result.doc:
/home/agentops/dev/md-manager-reviews/lane-repair-design.md

1. Recommendation: build operator-amend's apply path as `workflow repair "$RUN" <lane>[,<lane>] --commit <sha> --reason ...` (also `--dry-run`), plus risk-first's `--workspace` helper. The helper makes a detached worktree at the failing candidate or lane snapshot and writes a brief of the blocking reasons. `repair` never launches a session or runs the graph. The run continues with `automatic --live`, or `retry` for manual plans.
2. Scores out of 25: operator-amend 24, risk-first 20, worker-relaunch 18. The criteria are safety, crash recovery, operator simplicity, size and risk, and whether it would have saved 001.
3. I re-ran the checkpoint tests on copies of 001's `pipeline.sqlite` with langgraph 1.2.11. Updating the failed head is unsafe: it put `candidate` in the same step as the verifies, with new snapshots and old packets. Forking from the post-handoff checkpoint `1f1b78a9` (passing that checkpoint's `checkpoint_id`) gives next = the two verifies, `packets == {}`, and the candidate runs once after both. Forking a second time also works.
4. Rejected: risk-first's new thread per repair. It works, but its reasons for rejecting a same-thread fork do not hold, and every reader of the checkpoint would need to know which thread is current. Its ref name `repair-<n>` can collide with a legal lane id, and so can worker-relaunch's `<lane>-repair-<k>`. Use `refs/workflow-repair/<h16>/<n>/<lane>` instead.
5. The new snapshot is the lane's frozen tree plus the owned fix paths from the operator's commit, built with a private index. It is committed with parent = base and fixed dates, so a rerun after a crash gives the same commit. Freeze's ownership, symlink and no-op checks apply. `snapshots.json`, `plan.json` and all old evidence are never touched.
6. Attempts keep counting up: 001 would get worker:ui 2, candidate:controller 2 and candidate:ui 3. The 3-attempt limit becomes per lane, phase and repaired revision, capped at 3 repairs per run. The identical-failure check only compares attempts of the same revision, and it now logs an event. The rebuilt candidate goes to `candidate-<g>.json` and `candidate-<g>/`, with two new safety checks in `candidate()`.
7. `repair` refuses:
   - before freeze, and once a review bundle exists;
   - when a lock is held, or the source checkout has moved or is dirty;
   - when there is no blocked packet;
   - while an earlier repair is recorded but not applied.

   Crash recovery works through `repairs.json` (recorded, then applied): rerunning the identical command completes it with exactly one fork.
8. The viewer and export need no version bump in v1. Paused and controller events go on the timeline, the snapshot carries a `repair` object, and there is a `repair-<n>.diff`, a report section, `status.repairs` and a one-line note in the reviewer prompt.
9. Size for v1: about 370 production lines (a new `repair.py` of about 300, plus about 70 across `pipeline.py`, `automatic.py` and `__main__.py`), about 550 test lines, 15 tests including a real-Chromium 001 regression, and about 45 doc lines. That is roughly 1.5 days. The strict minimum that would have saved 001 is `--commit` only: about 260 lines and 9 tests.
10. Deferred:
    - Phase 2 is `repair --session --live`, the worker relaunch from the issue list: about +600 lines and 12 tests, after fix/autoupdate lands.
    - Phase 3 handles a lane blocked before freeze and replaces 312a96d, which should not be merged as it is.
    - Repair after review has started stays "start a new run".
